paragraphs.text: Dear sisters and elders, I had another great day today. I hope you did too. I really enjoyed speaking with each of the missionaries on the interviews. Lots of them asked if this would be the last interview with me. And I'm not sure about the answer to that question. I don't know for sure. It could be, but it might not be. But I did tell everyone and I'll tell all of you that no matter what, Sister Hughes and I will see each of you face-to-face before our mission ends. Hopefully a miracle will happen and we'll be able to have the old-fashioned zone conferences. We'll be able to get face-to-face that way. But if that doesn't happen, we'll come to every single apartment in the mission so that we can see each of you face-to-face. Because we want to. That's what we want. It's our selfish goal. We don't want to leave without being able to see each of you and look into your eyes person-to-person and let you know how much we love each one of you.

Well, I want to share something today about maybe how you can put some design on your life. So many people live their lives without a design. It's kind of like building a house without a plan. You're probably not going to like it very much and once you've got it all built, you're probably going to say, "Oh, I wish I'd remembered this and I wish I would have put something in on this." Well, it just won't be a very nice house. But if you use the proper process and you go out and you get a designer or an architect and you establish everything that you want on paper where it's easy to fix it and change it and move it around, and finally you look at that plan and you say, "Yeah, this is it. This is it. This is what we want." Then you go out and you actually build it physically and now you've got a house that is really, really close to what you see as your ideal or your perfect home. That's what you really want to do with your life. And yet there's not one person in a thousand who does that, which is probably why there are so many people who live lives that are just so, well, sad. They don't really want to be in that kind of a situation, but they don't really know how to avoid it. Most of the people that you and I run into that are living these kind of undesigned lives, they're good people. They work hard. They do the right thing as far as they understand how to do it, but they haven't done that critical key step of doing the deep thinking before they do the acting.

And so I want to share four questions. We have talked about these questions before, but I want to dig into them a little bit deeper on this recording, this podcast, so that you can begin to use this now. So you might say, "Well, I'm in the mission now." Well, yeah, but you're in the mission; you're going to be off the mission someday. And like, I think it was Amulek who says that same spirit which does possess your body at the time you leave this mortal world will have power to possess your body in the next life. And I would say that that person that you become in the mission field is the person you're going to be after the mission field. So why not build that person right now that you want to be in five years, ten years down the road?

All right. So the four questions a person has to resolve to get really clear about how they should move forward in their life are following here. But I want to break it out into two parts. Three of these questions have to be thought about very carefully and answered before a person even starts to go for that serious goal.

The first question is, what do I want? Simple question, right? But before you lose your focus, let me ask you, do you really know what you really, really want? Have you ever really dug deep in your mind and answered the question about what matters most to you? Many people live super shallow lives. They want to have something. Maybe it's a new car or a new computer or some other little short-term gadget or toy. Maybe they think, "I just want to have more money. If I had more money, then I'd be happy." There was a time when I thought that and I chased money for a while. But all it ever did was run away from me. When we chase things that are external possession-type things, we soon find that they run away from us or that if we get them, we find that they don't really make us very happy. And I think that that's a key thing to learn, and the sooner you learn it, the happier you're going to be. What these possessions really do, if we do get them, is they just become baggage that we have to carry around with us.

I was reading a little note about Elon Musk, the guy that is doing Tesla, the electric car. And I think he's got SpaceX and a bunch of other companies, a real bright entrepreneur. He's selling everything he has right now. He says, "I'm getting rid of everything. I'm getting rid of all my houses. I'm getting rid of everything. I'm getting rid of everything. I don't want to have these possessions. I want to get rid of all these possessions." I thought that was fascinating. And then he said later in the article, he says, "You know, that stuff just holds you back." How interesting. Very wealthy guy getting rid of all of his stuff because it holds him back. Well, that's the problem with answers to the question, "What do I want?" that start with the word "have." In other words, "I want to have this. I want to have that." That way of thinking is really short-term because possessions really don't make you happy for very long.

Now, there's another kind of answer to that big first question. And it is answers that start with the word "do." "I want to do this. I want to do that. I want to do the big job, then I'd be happy. I just don't want to do this little job. If I could do the big job that everybody else really wants to do, then I could do that and that would really be great, and life would be good." I've seen that that doesn't work very well either. "Do" is not a source of joy or happiness long-term. That's what I've found. The real answer to that first big question is: What do I want to be? What do I want to be? Once we have settled on what we want to be, it's pretty easy from there to go to what we want to do. And it's pretty easy from what we want to do to what we want to have. It actually just runs downhill so easily. But when we go "have," we still have to climb up to "do." And from "do," we have to climb up to "be." But if we just start at "be"—this is what I want to be—well, what is a person who is like that do? Well, there's your answer to "do." And what is a person who does that, what do they have? Well, there's what you have. And so as you look at it like this, you begin to realize that starting what do I want is: What do I want to be? What do I want to be?

Now we put ourselves in a position where we can actually answer the second question, which is: Why do I want to be that? If our "why" is not very clearly defined, if our "why" is not big, at least as big as our "what," we'll never have enough motivation to go get our "what." Because "why" is the source of motivation. "Why" is the passion. "Why" is what gets you up in the morning. "Why" is what keeps you up late at night. "Why" is the thing that makes you work hard all day long. "Why" is what causes you to put up with the fear of rejection. "Why" is what allows you to be mocked and still keep going forward. And so if you don't have that "why" clearly defined, or if you choose a goal of what you want to be and you just can't come up with a "why" that really feels strong to you, then honestly you need to come up with a new answer to question one. Because the "why" has to fit the "what." If the "why" doesn't fit the "what," you won't get the "what." Because the "why" is the engine that gets you to the place of the "what"—what you want to be.

So interestingly enough, once we've established why we want to be that kind of person, we begin to see real quickly that we can move into that third and most interesting question, which is: What am I willing to sacrifice to be that kind of person? Now this is, this is hard. This is hard because we don't like to sacrifice. We sing the song, "Sacrifice brings forth the blessings of heaven," but when it gets right down to us sacrificing that bad habit, or us sacrificing not saying that unkind word, or us sacrificing some of our precious "me time," well, it doesn't, doesn't feel so good. We don't want to make that sacrifice. We want somebody else to make that sacrifice, right? But the truth of the principle is that if you want to be, you've got to give up something that you are now. You can't stay where you are and go to where you want to be. It just doesn't work. And so this sacrifice question is one that takes some deep thought and some real honesty. And this is one of those places where lying to yourself is a disaster. You've got to be super honest with yourself. "I'm willing to give up this. I'm willing to give up that in order to be this."

Remember King Lamoni's father? Ammon's brother Aaron and his other brother went to see the great king and they taught him the gospel. And when the great king decided that there was something here that he really wanted to be converted to, he prayed to God and his prayer was very interesting: "And it came to pass that after Aaron had expounded these things unto him, the king said: What shall I do that I may have this eternal life of which thou hast spoken? Yea, what shall I do that I may be born of God, having this wicked spirit rooted out of my breast, and receive his Spirit, that I may be filled with joy, that I may not be cast off at the last day? Behold, said he, I will give up all that I possess, yea, I will forsake my kingdom, that I may receive this great joy." Close quote.

Interesting. So the king understood that sacrifice was necessary to achieve or gain something really important. And he was willing to make the sacrifice. Once you have decided what you want and why you want it, then you must decide what you're willing to give up to get it. The bigger the "be" goal that you have, the bigger the sacrifice you will have to make. People who think that they can get some great goal without paying a price for it are delusional. They're just not thinking rationally because it doesn't work that way in our universe. The good thing about sacrifice, however, is that it really isn't a sacrifice. It's not even a price. It's an investment. You are giving up something of lesser value that you have right now for something of greater value that you will be in the future. It requires faith to make the investment, but it is an investment. You wouldn't go from something of greater value to something of lesser value, not intentionally at least, right? No, you're giving up something of value X to get something of value 3X or 5X or 10X.

Once these three questions are answered honestly and with real intent, then you can move to the fourth question, which is: How am I going to become what I want to become? What are the steps I'm going to take to become that person I desire to be? "How" is about the process. You don't become in one step. Rather, it takes time and effort and usually many steps to reach that lofty goal of who you really want to be. And sometimes those steps are baby steps. Usually in the beginning, they're almost always baby steps, but you have to start taking them. You can't skip them. It was one step at a time, then the next step and the next step. And I've seen people who have tried to skip steps and they end up slipping and falling and have to start over at the beginning and go back and take the steps again.

Now, as I said at the outset at the beginning, each of you should be working on these questions right now in the mission field because the person you become in the mission field is the person you will be after the mission. At least in the first few months after you return home, you will reflect the kind of missionary you were in the final months of your mission. If you've set the right course for yourself in the mission, then you will naturally flow right into the next phase of your life without much challenge at all. In fact, it's been my observation that the most diligent and faithful missionaries had the easiest transition time back to life after the mission. They just didn't seem to have as big of problems as the missionaries who seemed to not be quite as diligent on their missions. That's not always the case, but that's generally the case. And it certainly doesn't surprise me that it's the case because if you've figured out the principles work in the mission field, you'll find that those same principles work after the mission.

Now, I'm hopeful that you have begun to see a little vision of who you could become while you've been serving here in the Quezon City North Mission. As you build on that vision and you ask God's help in refining it, you'll begin to see very clearly who you really are and who you could become. And elders and sisters, think big. Think big. Dream no small dreams. Make no small goals. Be a big dreamer. Be a big thinker. Your possibilities and your potential is vastly bigger than you think it is right now. I'm telling you that because I know you and I know a little bit about life. So think big.

Will it be hard work to get those big goals? Yes, it will be. It'll be hard work, but it'll also be deeply satisfying work. And you'll look back on your life after having thought big and acted big and you'll say, "I'm glad I did that. I'm glad I didn't spend my life down in the shallow part of the water. I'm glad I was able to learn how to swim in the deep water, how to play in the big leagues, how to be out there doing the big stuff." That way you can be of greater service to God and your fellow man because you've become someone who is really valuable in society. Imagine what power that will bring you and the church as you set your light on a hill so that people can see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven.
Elders and sisters, enjoy the rest of the evening and remember this day is the day the Lord has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it. Good night and sleep well. We love you.
